# What Our Tests Don't Prove
URL: https://bchir.github.io/the-ai-artisan-notes/articles/what-our-tests-dont-prove.html
Date: 2026-10-30 | Reading Time: 3 min | Author: Mohamed Amine Bchir
Synopsis: Unit, spec, and contract tests provide evidence for changes, but operational readiness still requires risk-based load and recovery checks.

This series began with a green build that did not deserve our confidence: an agent changed the implementation and its tests together, and both could share the same mistaken assumption.

> [!NOTE]
> **In brief:** Tests and quality gates strengthen evidence for a change, but operational readiness still needs risk-based checks and human judgment about acceptable risk.

The answer was not to abandon unit tests. It was to use different checks for different questions. Focused unit tests protect algorithms and invariants. Spec tests check agreed behavior through the application boundary. Contract tests check compatibility between services. Deterministic quality gates enforce the engineering standards we choose. Together, they give us stronger evidence about a change, while leaving human review focused on behavior, design, and risk decisions that need judgment.

But passing the reservation scenarios, including the concurrency case, does not show that the service will meet its latency and error-rate targets under peak traffic. Load and recovery checks can provide evidence about those operational risks. Choose them in proportion to the cost of failure, not as a checklist for every change.

A green build means the checks we chose passed. It is not a verdict on the whole system. We choose the standards, gather the evidence that matters, and accept the remaining risk.

## The series

1. [Unit Tests Are Dead. The Unit Moved.](../articles/ai-unit-tests-unit-moved.html)

# Deterministic Quality Gates for AI Code
URL: https://bchir.github.io/the-ai-artisan-notes/articles/deterministic-quality-gates-for-ai-code.html
Date: 2026-10-29 | Reading Time: 5 min | Author: Mohamed Amine Bchir
Synopsis: Deterministic quality gates let agents fix routine violations before review, so people can focus on behavior, design, and engineering decisions.

We built analyzers to tell us when code was getting harder to maintain. Then we ignored them.

Not because the warnings were always hard to understand, but because dealing with them cost time and attention. You stop the feature you were working on, switch context, inspect the warning, decide whether it matters, make a change, and rerun checks. When the task is already demanding and the warning is not blocking you, it is easy to defer it. Sometimes we simply could not be bothered. Then the warnings pile up, and the next person has even more noise to sort through.

An agent changes that trade-off. It can handle the repetitive loop of running the check, investigating the diagnostic, making a reasoned fix, and verifying it without asking a person to repeatedly abandon their work for each warning. That makes it practical to enforce standards more strictly than we often did before agents: checks that used to be advisory can become build-blocking gates, applied consistently rather than only when someone has time and patience to chase them.

This is not a reason to blindly promote every warning to an error. People still choose which standards matter, and agents still need guidance to address the design concern rather than silence the signal. The payoff is less human effort spent on routine cleanup and more attention available for behavior, architecture, and decisions that need judgment.

> [!NOTE]
> **In brief:** Deterministic quality gates let agents resolve repeatable engineering feedback before human review, freeing people to focus on design and decisions that need judgment.

## Choose gates that protect real decisions

A quality gate is useful when it enforces a decision the team actually values and gives feedback specific enough to act on. Depending on the stack and risk, that might be a complexity threshold, a forbidden dependency rule, a type check, or a security analyzer. Turning on every available warning is not a quality strategy; a noisy gate teaches people and agents to work around it.

The metric is not the goal. The quality decision behind it is.

## Choose and tune the checks

Quality gates do not have to be invented one rule at a time. For example, Microsoft's .NET SDK analyzers offer predefined analysis modes, including a `Recommended` mode, and let teams enable or tune rules by category or individual diagnostic. In other ecosystems, use the equivalent presets and per-rule configuration. Start with a useful baseline, then make the checks that matter to your project visible and enforceable.

As one concrete example, a shipping endpoint that accumulates checks for payment, inventory, destination, customs, and delivery can cross a configured cyclomatic-complexity limit. In .NET, CA1502 can report that threshold violation. The diagnostic is a signal to inspect the design, not an instruction to extract code mechanically. See Microsoft's documentation on [analysis modes and category configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/configuration-options) and the [CA1502 complexity rule](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/fundamentals/code-analysis/quality-rules/ca1502).

Put a short, tool-independent instruction in the repository's `AGENTS.md` so agents can apply it to any quality gate:

```markdown
When a quality gate fails:

- Identify what the check is intended to protect. Use its output, rule ID, category, documentation, failing test, and surrounding design as evidence.
- Decide whether the code has the underlying problem. If a sensible design change addresses it, make that change; do not just silence the diagnostic, move the violation, or game a metric.
- Re-run the relevant checks and tests. Confirm that the change fixed the concern without breaking behavior or creating the same problem elsewhere.
- Treat suppression or an exception as a last resort, only when the rule does not apply or conflicts with a sound design. Keep it narrow and justify why it is warranted.
```

For the complexity example, that means the agent first investigates whether the endpoint is combining unrelated shipping decisions. If payment, inventory, and delivery rules belong together, splitting them just to lower the count is metric gaming. If the endpoint really is coordinating distinct responsibilities, a focused policy or other design change may make the code easier to understand and maintain. The extracted logic and its behavior still need tests, and the gate still applies there. If the complexity is inherent and the rule is not useful in that case, the agent should explain why and propose a narrow, justified exception for review rather than take suppression as its first move.

That is the feedback loop: the check points to a concern; the agent investigates intent and design, makes a reasoned change, then reruns the gate and relevant tests. A green result confirms the configured threshold is met. It does not by itself prove the design improved, so the change remains reviewable by a person.

## Let agents close the feedback loop

The same principle applies beyond a compiler analyzer. A formatter or type checker can block a build; an architecture test can identify a forbidden dependency; a security check can report a vulnerable package. Whatever the tool, its result needs to reach the agent while it can still act on it. The agent should investigate the failure, make a reasoned change, and rerun the gate and relevant tests before handing the work to a reviewer. If a check only appears later in a dashboard or pull-request system, make sure the agent can retrieve it and the team agrees whether it blocks a merge.

For a new codebase, the team can start with a strict baseline. In a mature system, apply a rule to changed code first and expand it as existing debt is addressed. Either way, choose gates for the risks they reduce, keep their feedback actionable, and avoid enforcing thresholds for their own sake. A green check is not a design review; it is evidence that the configured boundary passed. Human review still matters. It can focus less on routine violations and more on choices the rules cannot make, while the code is held to a stricter, more consistent baseline.

# Contract Tests for AI-Generated Service Integrations
URL: https://bchir.github.io/the-ai-artisan-notes/articles/contract-and-integration-testing.html
Date: 2026-10-28 | Reading Time: 3 min | Author: Mohamed Amine Bchir
Synopsis: Contract tests verify that services agree on APIs and message schemas, catching incompatible integrations and invented interfaces in AI-generated code.

An inventory service may need product details from a Product Catalogue service, user information from a User service, or authorization from a Payment service. Each service can work correctly on its own and still fail when they communicate: the caller sends the wrong field, expects the wrong response, or publishes a message with a schema the consumer does not understand.

> [!NOTE]
> **In brief:** Contract tests check that service consumers and providers agree on APIs, messages, and schemas, catching compatibility errors that isolated tests and mocks can miss.

This is not a new problem caused by AI. Microservice teams have always needed to keep independently developed services compatible. AI makes the old problem easier to reproduce: an agent can confidently invent an endpoint, response shape, or event schema, then write a mock that agrees with the same invention. The local test passes; the real service does not.

## Check both sides of the agreement

A contract test checks compatibility between a consumer and provider. In a consumer-driven approach, the consumer records the interactions it relies on and the provider verifies it can honor them. With a provider-owned schema, consumers check their use against that published agreement. For messaging, producer and consumer must agree on the event schema and its evolution.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Inventory["Inventory service<br/>(consumer)"] -->|"API request"| Catalogue["Product Catalogue<br/>(provider)"]
    Contract["Contract test<br/>against agreed API or schema"]
    Contract -. verifies .-> Inventory
    Contract -. verifies .-> Catalogue
```

The contract needs grounding outside the generated client and its mock: an OpenAPI document, event schema, or consumer-driven contract verified against the provider. A document can be stale, so it is not evidence that the running provider conforms unless it is checked. These tests establish compatibility, not availability, authentication, timeout behavior, or resilience.

Tools such as [Pact](https://pact.io/) and [Microcks](https://microcks.io/) can help define and verify these agreements. The point here is not a tool tutorial: when an agent creates an integration, retain an independent compatibility check and watch for plausible but invented APIs and schemas.

The service-boundary spec from the previous article can use a mock server to keep a scenario controlled. Contract testing asks the next question: **does that mock represent a contract the real dependent service also honors?**

Contract tests address compatibility, not maintainability. A change can communicate correctly and still leave code that is hard to understand or extend. Next, we look at [how deterministic quality gates steer AI-generated code](../articles/deterministic-quality-gates-for-ai-code.html).

# Spec Tests at the Service Boundary
URL: https://bchir.github.io/the-ai-artisan-notes/articles/testing-real-service-boundaries.html
Date: 2026-10-27 | Reading Time: 6 min | Author: Mohamed Amine Bchir
Synopsis: Spec tests capture agreed service behavior in readable scenarios and run against the real application boundary, with examples and tooling across languages.

Readable, executable scenarios for expected behavior are not new. I’ll call them **spec tests** here. The change is in what we value: make them primary evidence for capability-level behavior, while keeping focused unit tests for algorithms and invariants.

> [!NOTE]
> **In brief:** Spec tests describe agreed capabilities in readable scenarios and verify them through the running service, independently of its internal design.

Imagine an agent is asked to add reservations. Before debating classes or methods, agree on the behavior: a customer can reserve available stock, an over-capacity request is rejected without changing inventory, and two customers competing for the last unit cannot both succeed.

Those promises can be written as readable, executable scenarios:

```gherkin
@inventory
Feature: Reserving available inventory

  Rule: A reservation cannot exceed available stock

    @hot_path
    Scenario: Reserve fewer units than are available
      Given a product has 2 units available
      When a customer reserves 1 unit
      Then the reservation is accepted
      And the available inventory is 1 unit

    @edge_case @expected_failure
    Scenario Outline: Reject a reservation above available inventory
      Given a product has <available> units available
      When a customer attempts to reserve <requested> units
      Then the request is rejected
      And the available inventory remains <available> units

      Examples:
        | available | requested |
        | 2         | 3         |
        | 1         | 2         |

    @edge_case
    Scenario: Reserve the exact available quantity
      Given a product has 2 units available
      When a customer reserves 2 units
      Then the reservation is accepted
      And the available inventory is 0 units

    @edge_case @concurrency
    Scenario: Two customers compete for the last unit
      Given a product has 1 unit available
      When two customers concurrently attempt to reserve 1 unit
      Then exactly one reservation is accepted
      And the other reservation is rejected
      And the available inventory is 0 units
```

These are spec tests: human-readable checks of agreed behavior. In .NET, Reqnroll can run scenarios written in Gherkin, but neither tool is a requirement. This approach is not specific to .NET: Cucumber supports languages including Java, JavaScript, and Ruby; Behave and pytest-bdd are options in Python; and godog brings Gherkin scenarios to Go. Choose the framework that fits the stack; the useful property is that people can review the promise and the test runner can execute it.

The tags classify the evidence: `@hot_path` marks the ordinary flow, `@edge_case` marks boundary conditions, `@expected_failure` marks rejected requests, and `@concurrency` identifies the race-condition check. They can help a team filter runs and see which kinds of behavior the suite covers. Reqnroll can map tags to test categories ([Gherkin reference](https://docs.reqnroll.net/latest/gherkin/gherkin-reference.html), [executing specific scenarios](https://docs.reqnroll.net/latest/execution/executing-specific-scenarios.html)).

The scenarios are not valuable just because they are written in plain language. Review them against the requirement: do they cover the important rules, are the outcomes right, and do they conflict with a capability the service already promises? This gives human review a compact place to focus on intended behavior, rather than asking reviewers to infer it from a large diff of implementation-coupled tests.

## Run the spec through the service

Run each scenario as a real caller would: through HTTP, a message endpoint, or another supported application boundary. For the rejection case, prepare a product with two units, send a request for three, check that the service rejects it, and verify that inventory remains at two. If the promise includes publishing an event, inspect it through a test broker or an observable outbox. A mock that verifies a method call does not prove the event was delivered or persisted.

Concurrency must be exercised, not just mentioned in a scenario: coordinate the two requests so they overlap, then verify both responses and the persisted inventory. Sequential requests would not expose the race. If the spec omits this guarantee, a passing suite leaves a black hole where the implementation can oversell.

Treat the service as a black box. Assert public behavior and relevant durable effects, not private class names, SQL text, or call order. The implementation can then change without making the capability—or the spec that describes it—meaningless.

To run scenarios against a separately hosted service, start the service and relevant dependencies as an environment before the test run. Aspire or Docker Compose can define and orchestrate it:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Agent["Coding agent"]
    Specs["Spec test suite"]

    subgraph Environment["Orchestrated environment · Aspire or Docker Compose"]
        direction LR
        Service["Real service"]
        Database[("Database")]
        Broker[("Message broker")]
        Redis[("Redis")]
        Mocks["Mock servers for<br/>external dependencies"]
        Service --> Database
        Service --> Broker
        Service --> Redis
        Service --> Mocks
    end

    Agent -->|"reads, adds, and runs"| Specs
    Specs -->|"HTTP / message boundary"| Service
    Environment -. "logs, metrics, and traces" .-> Diagnostics["OpenTelemetry diagnostics<br/>(Collector, observability stack, MCP)"]
    Diagnostics -. "failure evidence" .-> Agent
```

Use real dependencies when their behavior matters to the guarantee, such as a database, broker, or Redis. Use controlled mock servers for external systems that are not the subject of the scenario. The goal is not to recreate all of production; it is to exercise the capability across the boundary the spec claims to protect.

## Make failures diagnosable

Boundary tests have often been hard to work with: a bespoke harness could be fragile, and a failure might not reveal whether the problem was in the service, database, broker, or an external dependency. Unit tests are cheaper to run and give more localized feedback, which is why teams often favored them.

Orchestration tools such as Aspire and Docker Compose make it easier to start the service and dependencies together, wait for readiness, and exercise the running service as a black box. When a scenario fails, OpenTelemetry logs, metrics, and traces give the agent evidence to investigate, potentially through an MCP server. The same diagnostic path can help an SRE investigate an incident; in development, it can help an agent investigate a failing spec.

## A bonus: context for the next spec

The readable suite can also help an agent shape future work. If it already describes stock limits, retry behavior, and authorization, an agent asked to add bulk reservations can read those scenarios first. They show existing guarantees and help surface gaps or conflicts before the new behavior is proposed.

The agent can get that context from the feature files without tracing the implementation. Unlike a separate design document that may be superseded without being archived, the scenarios are executable checks the team expects to pass against the service. This does not make them correct or complete by themselves: when requirements change, update the affected specs and implementation together, and have people decide whether the proposed behavior is intended.

The suite records the behavior we agreed to protect; it cannot prove that we agreed on the right or complete behavior. Keep scenarios focused, free of implementation details, and runnable with isolated test data. And when mock servers stand in for external services, how do we know their assumptions match the real services? That is the question for [contract testing across service boundaries](../articles/contract-and-integration-testing.html).

# Unit Tests Are Dead. The Unit Moved.
URL: https://bchir.github.io/the-ai-artisan-notes/articles/ai-unit-tests-unit-moved.html
Date: 2026-10-26 | Reading Time: 7 min | Author: Mohamed Amine Bchir
Synopsis: AI can change implementation and its tests together. Learn how to shift code review toward agreed behavior and validate AI-assisted changes with separate checks.

You probably asked an AI agent to refactor legacy code. It changed the implementation, rewrote the unit tests, and reported a green build.

> [!NOTE]
> **In brief:** AI can make implementation and implementation-coupled tests agree while both miss user behavior. Review agreed specs and use checks at the boundaries that matter.

You may even have asked it to follow a TDD loop: write a failing test, implement the change, then run the tests. But the same agent chose both the implementation and what the tests should expect, from the same prompt and context, perhaps with the same mistaken assumption. That is feedback, not independent verification.

Then comes the diff: implementation and tests, line by line, file by file. You try to follow it. The PR stalls, or you keep reading past the point where you can tell whether the tests still protect the behavior.

That’s review exhaustion, not confidence: the tests may agree with the code and still fail to protect what users need.

So what should a human review instead?

Not every changed line. Let an AI review agent scan the implementation and report suspicious changes, missed cases, and likely defects. Treat its findings as leads, not certification; it can share the implementation agent’s assumptions. Then review the **spec tests**: a small set of human-readable checks that say what the system must do, in terms a user or business could recognize. They give us a compact place to review the behavior a change proposes. They can change alongside the implementation; when they do, reviewers should judge the changed behavior as a product decision, not treat it as routine test maintenance.

That’s when I started asking: **do the review habits and quality checks we’ve spent years building still fit work generated this way? And if they don’t, how should they evolve?**

We automated the implementation, and we kept the verification rituals built for hand-written implementation. That’s bolting a jet engine onto a horse cart and wondering why the ride feels strange.

So here’s my claim, and I’ll defend it:

**Unit tests aren’t dead because testing died. They’re dead because the unit moved.**

## A test can protect the wrong thing

We used to organize much of our confidence around the small pieces we wrote. Now an agent chooses those pieces for a capability and reshapes them in the next pass. Tests tied to methods and mocks can fail when the design changes; worse, the same agent can write implementation and tests from the same mistaken assumption. A green result can tell us the pieces agree, not that they meet the need.

We built the test pyramid around economics: unit tests were cheap, fast, and easy to diagnose, so we wrote many. AI makes producing tests cheaper. It does not make reviewing rewritten assertions free. The cost has shifted from writing tests to keeping the evidence trustworthy.

There is a token bill, too. People are rightly looking for ways to use fewer tokens, with tools like RTK and Caveman that compress context and reduce output. But we should also ask what those tokens buy. A single method may need normal, boundary, and failure unit tests, each with setup and assertions. If agents generate all of them from the same assumptions as the implementation, we still have to review them without gaining much confidence. When we target 80% to 90% line coverage mainly through unit tests, the test code could plausibly reach 50% to 200% of production code. That is my rough estimate, not a measured benchmark; coverage says what code ran, not whether the tests are good. The question is whether the tests earn their review and maintenance cost.

## What I’m proposing

Not a ban on unit tests, but a change in where confidence rests. Generated implementation is easy to reshape; trustworthy evidence is not. Keep tests tied to behavior, and update them when requirements change. The implementation alone should not force us to rewrite what users need.

Our work shifts with that change. We become spec developers: shaping, challenging, and maintaining the executable descriptions of the behavior we expect, while agents do more of the implementation work. That is not just writing scenarios. It is deciding what matters, what evidence would demonstrate it, and how the specification should evolve when the requirement changes.

Plain language does not make a spec correct. If it says one reservation succeeds when one item is available but says nothing about two customers arriving at once, the implementation has a blind spot: it may pass every written scenario and still oversell inventory. People must decide which concurrent outcomes, edge cases, and invariants are required; an agent can help propose them, but cannot certify its own interpretation.

## Complementary evidence, chosen by risk

The change is not “run more tests” or follow a fixed sequence. These practices answer different questions and complement one another. Choose the evidence that fits the change and its risks.

**Agree on behavior and review the design.** Define what must be true, then inspect the agent’s proposed component boundaries, data ownership, and failure handling before those choices spread through code. A design that exposes a missing requirement should send us back to the spec, not quietly redefine it.

**Test behavior at the relevant boundaries.** Keep focused unit tests for algorithms and invariants, and run spec tests through the real application boundary for capability-level guarantees that should remain meaningful as internals and design evolve. When intended behavior changes, revise the spec tests deliberately. See [spec tests at real application boundaries](../articles/testing-real-service-boundaries.html).

**Check compatibility between services.** Verify API, event, database, and provider assumptions with contract and integration tests; a local mock alone may agree with the same wrong assumption as the implementation. See [contract and integration testing](../articles/contract-and-integration-testing.html).

**Make repeatable quality rules executable.** Build, format, analyze, and enforce the quality and security expectations the repository has made explicit. See [how deterministic quality gates steer AI-generated code](../articles/deterministic-quality-gates-for-ai-code.html).

**Assess operational risk.** A payment or data migration may warrant representative load, failure, compatibility, rollout, and rollback checks. A small isolated change may not. This is not a new checklist: choose evidence by the cost of a missed failure. In the conclusion, [we consider what these checks still cannot prove](../articles/what-our-tests-dont-prove.html).

## Unit tests still matter

“Unit tests are dead” is a provocation, not a deletion command.

A tricky algorithm or security invariant still deserves focused tests. But a simple capability does not need twenty tests guarding private plumbing just because that is what we have always done.

Choose tests by risk. Not by ritual.

The smallest useful unit of confidence is not always a method or class. It is the behavior we agreed to protect.
